content: Economists use the term representative agent to describe a typical individual of a specific type, such as a typical consumer or a typical firm. In technical terms, an economic model is said to include a representative agent if all agents of the same type are identical. However, even when agents differ, economists sometimes refer to a model as having a representative agent if the aggregate of their decisions can be mathematically represented as the behavior of a single individual or a group of identical individuals. In contrast, models that include many different agents whose decisions cannot be aggregated in this way are referred to as heterogeneous agent models. The concept of the representative agent has historical roots dating back to the late 19th century. Francis Edgeworth introduced the term representative particular in 1881, while Alfred Marshall discussed the idea of a representative firm in his 1890 work, Principles of Economics. The concept gained greater prominence and controversy after Robert Lucas, Jr.'s critique of econometric policy evaluation in 1976. Lucas argued for the importance of microfoundations in macroeconomics, which led to the widespread adoption of representative agent models. Many modern macroeconomic models explicitly include optimization problems for representative agents, who may be consumers, producers, or both. The individual demand or supply curves derived from these models are often used as proxies for aggregate demand or supply curves. When economists analyze the behavior of a representative agent, it is typically because this approach simplifies the analysis by focusing on a single typical decision-maker rather than dealing with the complexity of many individual decisions. However, this assumption is abandoned when individual differences are central to the issue being studied. For instance, a macroeconomist might examine the effects of rising oil prices on a representative consumer, but analyzing health insurance would require a heterogeneous agent model. This is because health insurance inherently involves financial transfers from healthier individuals to those with costly medical needs. The prominence of representative agent modeling in macroeconomics can be partly attributed to the Lucas critique. Lucas argued that policy recommendations based on historical macroeconomic relationships might fail to account for behavioral changes by economic agents, which could alter those relationships. He proposed that models explicitly describing individual decision-making could address this issue. In such models, economists could simulate the effects of policy changes by recalculating the decisions of individual agents and aggregating them to assess macroeconomic outcomes. However, constructing such models with heterogeneous agents is technically challenging. As a result, early general equilibrium macroeconomic models often relied on the simplifying assumption of representative agents. While models with heterogeneous agents are more complex, they are becoming increasingly common in economic research. Critics of the representative agent approach, such as Hartley and Kirman, have raised significant concerns. Hartley finds the justifications for representative agent modeling unconvincing, while Kirman argues that these models ignore important aggregation issues and may commit the fallacy of composition. For example, a representative agent might make decisions that conflict with the preferences of all individuals in the economy. In such cases, policy recommendations based on the welfare of the representative agent would be invalid. Kirman concludes that reducing a group of heterogeneous agents to a single representative agent is not merely a convenient simplification but is fundamentally flawed and often leads to misleading or incorrect conclusions. He advocates for abandoning the representative agent approach, describing it as primitive and erroneous. Alternatives to the representative agent approach include agent-based simulation models, which can handle many heterogeneous agents, and dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models with heterogeneous agents. While constructing these models is challenging, they are becoming more prevalent in economic research.
